nameStory: Micrasterias furcata doesn't have a widely-used common name since it's a microscopic single-celled organism that most people never see! The scientific name comes from Greek words meaning 'little star' (Micrasterias) and 'forked' (furcata), describing its beautiful star-like shape with branching lobes that fork at the tips.
description: This isn't actually a plant at all, but a tiny single-celled organism called a desmid that lives in freshwater. It's so small you need a microscope to see it, but when you do, it looks like a flattened green star or snowflake with intricate lobes and branches. Each cell is perfectly symmetrical, split down the middle like it was designed by nature's own architect. These microscopic beauties are actually algae that help keep our ponds and lakes healthy.

idTips.label: Star-like Shape
idTips.description: Under a microscope, appears as a flattened, symmetrical star with multiple lobes radiating from the center, like a living snowflake

idTips.label: Forked Tips
idTips.description: The outer edges of each lobe split into two or more pointed tips, giving it that characteristic 'furcata' or forked appearance

idTips.label: Green Color
idTips.description: Bright green due to chlorophyll, the same pigment that makes plants green - it's photosynthetic like a tiny plant

idTips.label: Perfect Symmetry
idTips.description: Each half mirrors the other exactly, with a clear division line down the middle where the two halves meet

idTips.label: Microscopic Size
idTips.description: Invisible to the naked eye - you'll need at least 100x magnification to see its intricate details clearly

habitat: Found in clean, still or slow-moving freshwater like ponds, quiet lake edges, and boggy areas throughout New England. Prefers slightly acidic water with low nutrients, often in association with sphagnum moss and other desmids. Look for them in pristine woodland ponds and undisturbed wetlands where water quality is high.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water warms and daylight increases. Best time to find them as they multiply rapidly in clean, cool spring waters.
seasonality.summer: Most abundant during warm months when photosynthesis is at peak. May be harder to spot in very warm, nutrient-rich water where other algae dominate.
seasonality.fall: Still present but populations may decline as temperatures drop and daylight decreases. Often easier to observe as competing algae die back.
seasonality.winter: Present but dormant in cold water. Populations are at their lowest, though some individuals persist under ice in deeper water bodies.

funFact: Each Micrasterias cell is like a living crystal - when it reproduces, each half grows a brand new matching half, creating two identical star-shaped daughters that are perfect mirror images of the parent, making them some of nature's most precise biological sculptures!
confusionNotes: Under the microscope, it might be confused with other star-shaped desmids, but the distinctly forked tips of the lobes are the giveaway - remember 'furcata means forked' to distinguish it from rounder or smoother-edged relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called algae, desmids like Micrasterias are quite different from the slimy green algae most people know - they're actually closer to land plants evolutionarily and are considered living jewels of the microscopic world, prized by naturalists for their geometric beauty.
compareHints: Micrasterias furcata stands out from its relatives by having distinctly forked lobe tips, while species like M. rotata have more rounded edges and M. truncata has cut-off or squared ends to its lobes. The forked tips are your best clue - they're more pronounced and numerous than in most other Micrasterias species found in New England waters.
